blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
DNA :-
    • The double helix model of DNA, proposed by Watson and Crick, consists of two complementary, antiparallel strands that form a right-handed helical structure.
    • The backbone is made of deoxyribose sugar and phosphate groups, with nitrogenous bases (adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine) facing inward.
    • Base pairing occurs through hydrogen bonds: adenine pairs with thymine (2 bonds), and cytosine pairs with guanine (3 bonds).
    • Each turn of the helix contains about 10 base pairs, with a spacing of 0.34 nm between them.
    • The structure has major and minor grooves, essential for protein interactions, and it follows Chargaff's rule (A=T, C=G). This stable and elegant design allows for efficient genetic storage, replication, and transcription.

blocks.title: Chargaff’s Equivalence Rule
blocks.text:
NCERT Question:
If a double stranded DNA has 20 per cent of cytosine, calculate the percent of adenine in the DNA.
Ans. A = 30%

Sol. According to Chargaff's Rule:

A + G =T + C

If C = 20% then G = 20%

So,  G + C = 40%

Rest  A + T = 100 - 40 = 60%

Therefore, T = A = 60/2 = 30%

rows: More stable & less reactive due to deoxyribose sugar and presence of thymine instead of uracil
Less stable & more reactive due to presence of ribose sugar & also catalytic function
Depends on RNA for expression through synthesis of protein
Can directly code for synthesis of protein.
Both RNA and DNA can function as genetic material, but DNA being more stable is preferred for storage of genetic information. For the transmission of genetic information, RNA is better.

blocks.text:

rows: Confusing the Types of Bacterial Strains Used in Griffith experiment
Students may mix up the smooth (S) and rough (R) strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae used in Griffith’s experiment.

Griffith used two types of bacterial strains:The S strain (smooth) is virulent because it has a capsule that helps it evade the host immune system.The R strain (rough) is non-virulent because it lacks the capsule and cannot cause disease.
Believing Griffith Discovered DNA as the Transforming Principle
Students  may mistakenly believe that Griffith directly concluded that DNA was the transforming principle from his experiment.

While Griffith’s experiment showed that something from the dead S strain transformed the R strain into a virulent form, he did not identify that substance as DNA. It was later experiments, particularly by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty in 1944, that identified DNA as the transforming principle.

blocks.question:
Which scientist conducted an experiment with P32 and S35 labelled phages for demonstrating that DNA is the genetic material?

(2) A. D Hershey and M.J. Chase

(3) F. Griffith

(4) O.T. Avery, C.M. MacLeod and M. McCarty
blocks.answer:
Ans. (2)

Explanation

Hershey and Chase conducted the famous blender experiment in 1952 using bacteriophage labeled with radioactive isotopes.

Phosphorous - 32 to label DNA

Sulfur - 35 to label proteins

Their experiment demonstrated that DNA, not protein, is the genetic material transmitted by viruses to bacteria.

(2) A. D Hershey and M.J. Chase
(4) O.T. Avery, C.M. MacLeod and M. McCarty

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
DNA REPLICATION :-

$ \text { DNA } \xrightarrow{\text { Replication }} \text { DNA } $

Semiconservative DNA Replication :-

• Proposed by - Watson & Crick (specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism)
    • Experimentally proved by - Meselson & Stahl $\rightarrow $ in E.coli using heavy isotope of Nitrogen

blocks.title: Mechanism of DNA Replication
blocks.text:
Machinery & Enzymes of DNA Replication :-

• DNA-dependent DNA polymerase

• Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates: dual purpose -act as substrate & also as an energy source for the polymerisation reaction.
    • DNA Ligase: joins the discontinuously synthesised strands.

blocks.title: Important Points
blocks.text:
• Origin of Replication: A definite region in DNA where the replication begins
    • The replication occurs within a small opening of the DNA helix referred to as the Replication fork.
    • On one strand, the replication is continuous (the template with polarity 3' to 5'), while on the other, it is discontinuous (the template with polarity 5' to 3').

blocks.text: The process of copying genetic information from one strand of the DNA into RNA is termed as transcription.

blocks.title: Question 1
blocks.question:
AGGTATCGCAT is a sequence from the coding strand of a gene. What will be the corresponding sequence of the transcribed mRNA?

(1) AGGUAUCGCAU

(2) UGGTUTCGCAT

(3) ACCUAUGCGAU

(4) UCCAUAGCGUA
blocks.answer:
Ans. (1)

  • DNA Coding Strand (Given):
The given sequence is AGGTATCGCAT.      • The coding strand of DNA has the same sequence as the mRNA, except that in RNA, thymine (T) is replaced by uracil (U).
  • mRNA Sequence:      • Replace T with U in the given sequence.
      • The resulting mRNA sequence is: AGGUAUCGCAU.
  • Additional Details:      • The template strand (non-coding strand) of DNA is complementary to the mRNA, but it is not needed here since the coding strand directly provides the sequence for mRNA.

blocks.title: Question 2
blocks.question:
Which of the following is the correct sequence of events in transcription?

a) Initiation → Elongation → Termination
b) Elongation → Initiation → Termination
c) Termination → Elongation → Initiation
d) Initiation → Termination → Elongation
blocks.answer:
a) Initiation → Elongation → Termination

The correct sequence of events in transcription is initiation, elongation, and termination:

  • Initiation
The RNA polymerase enzyme attaches to the promoter of a gene, signaling the DNA to unwind.
  • Elongation
The RNA polymerase moves along the DNA template strand, adding nucleotides to the mRNA strand.
  • Termination
The RNA polymerase transcribes the terminator sequence in the gene, detaching from the DNA and ending transcription.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: The relationship between the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain and the nucleotide sequence of DNA or m-RNA is called genetic code.

columns: - Universal: The same in nearly all organisms. - Degenerate: Multiple codons can code for the same amino acid. - Non-overlapping: Codons are read one after another without overlapping. - Commaless: No punctuation between codons. - Unambiguous: Each codon specifies one amino acid. - Start and Stop Signals: Start codon: AUG (Methionine). Stop codons: UAA. UAG. UGA.
rows: - Sense codons: 61 codons that code for amino acids. - Stop codons 3 codons (UAA UAG. UGA) that signal the end of transiation. - Structure: Triplets of nucleotides (A U, G, C). - Wobble Hypothesis: The third base in the codon often does not affect the amino acid it codes for, explaining degeneracy.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Translation is the process by which ribosomes synthesize proteins using mRNA as a template.

blocks.title: Steps of Translation
blocks.text:
Steps of Translation

(1) ACTIVATION OF AMINO ACID

(2) CHARGING OF t–RNA (Loading of t-RNA or Aminoacylation of tRNA)

(3) TRANSLATION :

3 steps :–

(a) Initiation of polypeptide chain

(b) Chain – Elongation

(c) Chain – Termination

rows: Amino acids are attached to their corresponding tRNA molecules by the enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.
- mRNA near the start codon (AUG)- Initiator tRNA carrying Methionine (in eukaryotes) binds to AUG codon.- Large ribosomal subunit joins to form the complete initiation complex.

- Codon Recognition: The tRNA carrying the correct amino acid pairs its anticodon with the mRNA codon.- Peptide Bond Formation: The ribosome catalyzes the formation of a peptide bond between the amino acids in the P site and A site.- Translocation: The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon, shifting the tRNA from the A site to the P site, and the empty tRNA moves to the E site.
- Stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) enters the A site.- Release factors bind to the ribosome, causing the release of the polypeptide chain.- The ribosomal subunits dissociate from the mRNA.
- The newly synthesized polypeptide chain folds into its functional 3D structure.- Post-translational modifications like phosphorylation, glycosylation, or cleavage may occur.

blocks.text: The mechanism which stimulates the expression of certain genes and inhibits that of others is called regulation of gene expression.

rows: Controls the breakdown of lactose in E. coli by producing enzymes (β-galactosidase, permease, and transacetylase).
lacZ (codes for β-galactosidase), lacY (codes for permease), lacA (codes for transacetylase).
O: A region where the repressor binds to prevent transcription when lactose is absent.
P: The site where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription of the lac genes.
Allolactose (a metabolite of lactose) is the inducer that inactivates the repressor, allowing transcription to occur.
Produced by the lacl gene, binds to the operator site in the absence of lactose, preventing transcription.

When lactose is present, it is converted to allolactose, which binds to the repressor, changing its shape and preventing it from binding to the operator site. This allows RNA polymerase to transcribe the genes.
In some mutants (e.g., lacl'), the repressor protein is nonfunctional, leading to constant expression of lac genes.
When glucose is available, it prevents the activation of the lac operon even if lactose is present (via cAMP-CAP complex).
The lac operon is off when lactose is absent (repressor bound to operator), and on when lactose is present (repressor inactivated by allolactose).

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• It is a technique to identify a person on the basis of his/her DNA specificity.
  • This technique was invented by Sir Alec Jeffreys in 1984.
  • Introduced by Dr. V.K. Kashyap & Dr. Lal Ji Singh ( In India)

blocks.title: Steps of DNA Fingerprinting
blocks.text:
(i) Isolation of DNA

(ii) Digestion of DNA by restriction endonucleases

(iii) Separation of DNA fragments by electrophoresis

(iv) Transferring (blotting) of separated DNA fragments to synthetic membranes, such as nitrocellulose or nylon

(v) Hybridisation using labelled VNTR probe

(vi) Detection of hybridised DNA fragments by autoradiography

blocks.title: Flow chart of steps of DNA Fingerprinting

rows: DNA is collected from biological samples (eg- blood. saliva, hair, skin cells).
DNA is extracted from the collected sample using chemical or mechanical methods to isolate the genetic material.
Restriction enzymes are used to cut the DNA into smaller fragments at specific sequences.
DNA fragments are separated by size using an electric field, where smaller fragments move faster through the gel.
The separated DNA fragments are transferred from the gel onto a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane for further analysis.
DNA probes, which are labeled with radioactive or fluorescent markers, bind to specific DNA fragments on the membrane.
The pattern of bands formed by the hybridized DNA fragments is analyzed to create the DNA fingerprint.
The banding patterns are compared to reference samples or used to identify genetic relationships or individual identity.

blocks.title: Applications of DNA Fingerprinting
blocks.text:
• In forensic science
    • Paternity testing in case of disputes
    • In determining population & genetic diversities

blocks.title: Important points and Features of Human Genome
blocks.text:
• (i) The human genome contains 3164.7 million base pairs.
    • (ii) The average gene consists of 3000 bases, but sizes vary greatly, with the largest known human gene being dystrophin at 2.4 million bases (bp).
    • (iii) The total number of genes is estimated at 30,000-much lower than previous estimates of 80,000 to 1,40,000 genes. Almost all (99.9 per cent) nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all people.
    • (iv) The functions are unknown for over 50 per cent of discovered genes.
    • (v) Less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins.
    • (vi) Repeated sequences make up very large portion of the human genome.
    • (vii) Repetitive sequences are stretches of DNA sequences that are repeated many times, sometimes hundred to thousand times. They are thought to have no direct coding functions, but they shed light on chromosome structure, dynamics and evolution.
    • (ix) Scientists have identified about 1.4 million locations where single-base DNA differences (SNPs- single nucleotide polymorphism, pronounced as 'snips') occur in humans, this information promises to revolutionise the processes of finding chromosomal locations for disease- associated sequences and tracing human history.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
DNA :-
    • The double helix model of DNA, proposed by Watson and Crick, consists of two complementary, antiparallel strands that form a right-handed helical structure.
    • The backbone is made of deoxyribose sugar and phosphate groups, with nitrogenous bases (adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine) facing inward.
    • Base pairing occurs through hydrogen bonds: adenine pairs with thymine (2 bonds), and cytosine pairs with guanine (3 bonds).
    • Each turn of the helix contains about 10 base pairs, with a spacing of 0.34 nm between them.
    • The structure has major and minor grooves, essential for protein interactions, and it follows Chargaff's rule (A=T, C=G). This stable and elegant design allows for efficient genetic storage, replication, and transcription.

rows: Confusing the Types of Bacterial Strains Used in Griffith experiment
Students may mix up the smooth (S) and rough (R) strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae used in Griffith’s experiment.

Griffith used two types of bacterial strains:The S strain (smooth) is virulent because it has a capsule that helps it evade the host immune system.The R strain (rough) is non-virulent because it lacks the capsule and cannot cause disease.
Believing Griffith Discovered DNA as the Transforming Principle
Students  may mistakenly believe that Griffith directly concluded that DNA was the transforming principle from his experiment.

While Griffith’s experiment showed that something from the dead S strain transformed the R strain into a virulent form, he did not identify that substance as DNA. It was later experiments, particularly by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty in 1944, that identified DNA as the transforming principle.

rows: Amino acids are attached to their corresponding tRNA molecules by the enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.
- mRNA near the start codon (AUG)- Initiator tRNA carrying Methionine (in eukaryotes) binds to AUG codon.- Large ribosomal subunit joins to form the complete initiation complex.

- Codon Recognition: The tRNA carrying the correct amino acid pairs its anticodon with the mRNA codon.- Peptide Bond Formation: The ribosome catalyzes the formation of a peptide bond between the amino acids in the P site and A site.- Translocation: The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon, shifting the tRNA from the A site to the P site, and the empty tRNA moves to the E site.
- Stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) enters the A site.- Release factors bind to the ribosome, causing the release of the polypeptide chain.- The ribosomal subunits dissociate from the mRNA.
- The newly synthesized polypeptide chain folds into its functional 3D structure.- Post-translational modifications like phosphorylation, glycosylation, or cleavage may occur.

O: A region where the repressor binds to prevent transcription when lactose is absent.
P: The site where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription of the lac genes.
Allolactose (a metabolite of lactose) is the inducer that inactivates the repressor, allowing transcription to occur.
Produced by the lacl gene, binds to the operator site in the absence of lactose, preventing transcription.

When lactose is present, it is converted to allolactose, which binds to the repressor, changing its shape and preventing it from binding to the operator site. This allows RNA polymerase to transcribe the genes.
In some mutants (e.g., lacl'), the repressor protein is nonfunctional, leading to constant expression of lac genes.
When glucose is available, it prevents the activation of the lac operon even if lactose is present (via cAMP-CAP complex).
The lac operon is off when lactose is absent (repressor bound to operator), and on when lactose is present (repressor inactivated by allolactose).

blocks.title: Flow chart of steps of DNA Fingerprinting

rows: DNA is collected from biological samples (eg- blood. saliva, hair, skin cells).
DNA is extracted from the collected sample using chemical or mechanical methods to isolate the genetic material.
Restriction enzymes are used to cut the DNA into smaller fragments at specific sequences.
DNA fragments are separated by size using an electric field, where smaller fragments move faster through the gel.
The separated DNA fragments are transferred from the gel onto a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane for further analysis.
DNA probes, which are labeled with radioactive or fluorescent markers, bind to specific DNA fragments on the membrane.
The pattern of bands formed by the hybridized DNA fragments is analyzed to create the DNA fingerprint.
The banding patterns are compared to reference samples or used to identify genetic relationships or individual identity.
